On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya held all the power: sword in hand, he ordered Sitaram to open the locked door, and when Sitaram hesitated out of duty, Udayaditya threatened force. Sitaram—loyal because Udayaditya had twice saved his life—refused to fight him and instead submitted, begging to be disarmed and bound so the Maharaj would spare him. Udayaditya overpowered and tied him up and went free.

On the night of Udayaditya's own escape, the roles invert completely. Sitaram is now the rescuer and commander: he opens the prison door amid the fire and almost carries the long-confined Udayaditya out. Udayaditya, once the decisive leader, has become passive and helpless—disoriented by open space, he asks Sitaram, "What should I do? Where should I go?" and meekly follows his lead. The guard who once bound himself at the prince's feet now leads the prince to freedom, while the prince who once commanded him now depends entirely on him.

Pratapaditya first ordered two Pathans to murder Basanta Ray at the Simultali inn on his way to Jessore; one Pathan lured away his retainers with a false dacoit alarm, but the other relented and revealed the plot. Basanta Ray was finally killed after Muktiyar Khan and soldiers entered Raigarh in disguise, captured Udayaditya, presented Pratapaditya’s written death order, and had Abdul behead the old king with a sword.
In Jessore’s palace inner quarters, disguised as a middle-aged woman; in Chandradwip’s palace, undisguised as the court jester.

Rukmini, living in disguise as the widow Mangala, secretly prepared a poison—solicited by the Mahishi through Matangini as "medicine" to win Udayaditya's heart away from Surma—which killed Surma before her exile could take place. Her departure was thus caused by murder, disguised to look like suicide by her own hand.

Because Vibha refused to go with Rammohan the first time, the humiliated King Ramchandra Ray decided to take revenge by marrying another wife. When Vibha finally arrived at Chandradwip, it was on the very day of the king's new wedding — there was no longer any place for her in her own royal palace, and all her hopes of happiness were shattered, causing her to faint in grief upon hearing the news.

Rukmini tricked Udayaditya into giving her the signet ring from his finger during a stormy-night visit. Since the ring bore the Yubaraj's name engraved as a seal, Sitaram and Bhagavat used it to stamp a forged petition in which Udayaditya appeared to accuse Pratapaditya of treason to the Emperor in Delhi to seize the kingdom. Bhagavat then delivered this petition directly to Pratapaditya, claiming a servant of Udayaditya had been carrying it toward Delhi. Though skeptical of its authenticity, Pratapaditya used it as justification to order Udayaditya's imprisonment, ostensibly to have guards prevent any secret plots.

Because Ramchandra Ray's midnight escape could only happen when Udayaditya forced his way out of the locked inner quarters—overpowering and tying up the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat—Pratapaditya dismissed those guards from palace service. Learning of their resulting destitution, Udayaditya granted them a monthly stipend, which enraged Pratapaditya, who forbade anyone to aid them on pain of being considered against his will. Surma then secretly continued sending the stipends through a trusted maid, who disclosed it to Mangala. When this defiance reached Pratapaditya's ears, he sent word to the inner quarters that Surma must leave for her paternal home—thus the exile decree.

The song is a poignant lament of loneliness and loss—an old man's cry that everything he once had is gone, leaving only emptiness, with no loved ones left to answer his call. Basanta Ray sings it first alone on the veranda of his Raigarh palace at sunset, humming to himself as he grieves for the dear ones in Jessore he may never see again; he sings it again in Jessore, standing before Surma's silent, empty, desolate room after learning of Udayaditya's imprisonment, taking Vibha's hand and slowly giving voice to the family's ruin.

Rukmini discovered the escape and raced to the canal, but Sitaram blocked her and the boatmen pulled her off, so the boat carrying Udayaditya and Basanta Ray got away; even her suicide leap into the canal failed. Surviving, she went before Pratapaditya and revealed everything—that the Yubaraj had escaped with the old King of Raigarh, exposing the fabricated death-by-fire—and then led the king's men to Raigarh, where she pointed out Udayaditya in the field to Muktiyar Khan's soldiers. With Udayaditya captured, Pratapaditya's secret death order against Basanta Ray was carried out, and the old king was executed that same evening.

Pratapaditya's reception of his son-in-law was marked by deliberate restraint and quiet indifference: no path was lit, no Nabat played, and only the Dewan came to welcome Ramchandra—belatedly, with a small retinue and a small elephant. In their meeting, Pratapaditya remained calm and unhurried, showing neither joy nor insult, turning instead to routine royal business with his minister and dismissing Ramchandra with a simple "Go now, my boy, to the inner quarters." Through this understated composure, Ramchandra perceived Pratapaditya's genuine superiority.

Later, in his own court, Ramchandra answers Pratapaditya's status with petty, theatrical denigration: daily mockery sessions where courtiers and the jester Ramai Bhand deride Pratapaditya as a mere two-generation upstart—"son of a leech," whose father had to beg Ramchandra's grandfather for the royal anointment—and where even discussing Pratapaditya and Ramchandra in the same breath is treated as a crime. Thus Pratapaditya's dignified silence and effortless authority stand in contrast to Ramchandra's insecure, small-minded need to publicly belittle his father-in-law to inflate his own honor.

Rukmini changes her name to Mangala and settles near Jessore, cultivating palace contacts and plotting to possess Udayaditya. When the Rajmahishi secretly seeks a medicine to detach him from Surma, Rukmini supplies poison, which kills Surma. Afterward, Rukmini confronts the grief-stricken Udayaditya, blames him for her ruin, demands his love, and takes his ring, renewing her attempt to ensnare him.

In his youth, Udayaditya wished he had never been born crown prince, believing royal birth brought him only scrutiny, his father's contempt, and failure at governing (his lenient rule of the Hosenkhali pargana convinced the court he could never rule). This lifelong sense of unworthiness culminates after the disaster at Raigarh: journeying back as a prisoner, he despairs over the ruin caused for his sake and resolves to leave the world. Brought before Pratapaditya, he declares himself unworthy and begs release from the throne, then formalizes his renunciation by swearing at Ma-Kali's feet, before his father, that he will never accept even an iota of Jessore's kingdom, sit on its throne, or touch its scepter—naming Samaraditya as heir—and leaves for Kashi to live as an ascetic, founding a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name.

Ramchandra Ray's letter renouncing Vibha—declaring she should not be sent to Chandradwip again—was entrusted to the old messenger Nayanchand. Fearing Pratapaditya's wrath if the letter reached him, Nayanchand delivered it instead to the Mahishi, who dared not tell Vibha (the delicate girl would not survive it) or the Maharaj, and kept it secret. Later she showed it to Basanta Ray, who advised her not to reveal it to anyone and suggested, believing Ramchandra had written it only out of temporary anger, that she announce in the household that Ramchandra had written requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip—so that Vibha would not object to going. The Mahishi did exactly this, telling Vibha and the household that the letter was a summons asking for her to be sent to her in-laws' house. Misled into believing her husband had understood her and was lovingly calling her back, Vibha was overcome with joy, regained her cheerfulness, and began eagerly awaiting her departure.

Pratapaditya ordered the canal beside the palace blocked with large sal-wood logs, trapping Ramchandra's boat. But Rammohan and his men physically hauled the boat up and over the logs while the guards' stones fell short, their only gun lacked flintlock and ammunition, and the man sent for a pursuit boat dawdled—stopping to smoke tobacco and press a debt—so the chase came too late and Ramchandra escaped to the Bhairav river.

Basanta Ray's sitar mirrors his despair over Udayaditya. When forced to part from Udayaditya, he tried to play his beloved sitar furiously, but his tears blurred his eyes and his throat choked until he had to put it down; departing, he left the instrument behind, saying he would never play it again. Later, in exile at Raigarh, the sitar—his "eternal companion"—was no longer with him, and he gazed at the setting sun singing a desolate song: "I alone am left behind... what remains is only emptiness." When Khan Saheb asked about the instrument, he answered that the sitar was still there, "only its strings have broken, and it can no longer be tuned"—an image of his own broken spirit. The abandoned, untunable sitar and the joyless singing that rose spontaneously to his lips expressed how, with Udayaditya taken from him (and later imprisoned), all joy had drained from his life: he still had song, but no one to sing for and no happiness in singing.

Udayaditya was once fearless and openly championed oppressed subjects, intervening to protect them regardless of the consequences. After Surma’s death, grief and a paralyzing dread of Pratapaditya destroy his resolve: he abandons the planned rescue at Chhapra, hides from a subject being beaten, and never sends promised aid to Bhagavat and Sitaram. Though still compassionate, he is too intimidated and hesitant to act.

Sitaram undoes the harm—Udayaditya's imprisonment, which resulted from the forged petition—by exploiting a fire that broke out near the palace. While the guards abandoned their posts to save their belongings, he opened the prison door, warned Udayaditya that the prison was on fire, pulled him out, and led him away to freedom, taking him to Basanta Ray.

Rammohan twists large sheets into a rope, anchors it to a rooftop pillar, carries Ramchandra on his back down toward the boat, grips the rope with his teeth, lowers him with both hands, and then jumps aboard. Later, he lifts the unconscious Vibha bodily out of Ramchandra’s palace, places her in a waiting palanquin, and returns to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed as a cherished princess: her mother decks her in thick gold bangles, huge diamond bracelets, a large nose ring, and an elaborate hairstyle, while she glows with barely concealed joy at receiving her husband. In Chandradwip, she strips away all royal presentation, refuses a palanquin, dresses like a common woman, and enters unrecognized like a maidservant or beggar. Abandoning queenly dignity, she falls at Ramchandra’s feet—not to seek alms, but humbly to surrender everything and leave.

In his bedchamber after Surma's death, the window is a site of grief and absence—he sits there leaving Surma's usual spot empty, gazing at the same moonlight, garden, and breeze, aching with the impossible hope that she might still appear. In the prison cell, the small window transforms into a symbol of freedom and hope: seeing the sky and flying birds through it, he believes his own cage will one day break, that he too will swim freely in the endless sky. Away from the window he sees only darkness and forgets he will be liberated; at the window he knows he is "naturally free" and beyond any king's power. Thus the window shifts from evoking what he has lost to affirming the liberty he still possesses within.

Sitaram, a penniless but stylish guard, was drawn to the widow Rukmini for both her beauty and her money, regularly borrowing cash from her under the pretense of witty flirtation and feigned affection — calling her "Pranpriye" while never repaying her, and she, secretly plotting with him, indulged the arrangement.

The dynamic shattered when Sitaram held Rukmini responsible for Udayaditya's imprisonment. Enraged, he went to her hut, cursed her, nearly struck her, and swore to burn her house, grind her face on the floor, blacken her face with lime and soot, and drive her from the city. Rukmini met this with a barely contained, demonic fury, vowing that only she could help or harm "her" Yubaraj.

The turn to mortal danger came after Sitaram engineered Udayaditya's escape through a staged prison fire. Assuming Mangala was dead, he slipped to her cottage that night to steal her money — only to find her alive, dripping wet, ashen-faced, having "returned from the door of Yama." Mistaking her for a ghost, he froze, then tried his old tactic of feigned affection. But Rukmini, now reckless and stripped of all hope, swore to see him and the Yubaraj burned on pyres, and fetched a curved blade to kill him. Sitaram fled the cottage and that same night abandoned Jessore for Raigarh, knowing she could expose everything — which she promptly did, denouncing him before Pratapaditya as the arsonist behind the escape.

The fire began in the guards' living quarters near the prison, timed so the guards—already lax because Udayaditya never tried to flee—abandoned their posts to save their belongings, leaving Sitaram free to pull Udayaditya from his cell. Sitaram's men, embedded among the firefighters, sabotaged the effort by pouring water where there was no fire, breaking water pots, and creating confusion, so the blaze raged on and occupied everyone. While the chaos continued, his men set the now-empty prison cell ablaze piece by piece—windows, doors, beams, rafters—until the roof collapsed, and Sitaram threw bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's own sword (taken from him at the boat) into the burning room. Staged shouts then drew the guards to the cell: a man cried that the Yubaraj's cell was burning, another claimed screams were heard from inside, and Sitaram himself announced the roof had collapsed with no response from the prisoner. This manufactured a death scene complete with planted evidence and false witnesses, so that Sitaram could spread the news that Udayaditya had perished in the fire and remain untroubled. The ruse initially worked—Pratapaditya's court heard testimony of a witness who "saw" the Yubaraj through the window, others who heard screams, and the melted sword remains produced as proof—until Rukmini exposed Sitaram's plot and a fisherman's report of Udayaditya traveling downriver confirmed the escape.

In his own court, Ramchandra Ray shows no gratitude and instead joins his courtiers in mocking and ridiculing Udayaditya—for no crime other than being Pratapaditya's son. He dismisses Udayaditya's life-saving act as something that was bound to happen, and convinces himself that Udayaditya only acted for the sake of his own sister, so saving his life was not really Udayaditya's main objective.

Pratapaditya scoffs at his minister's warnings about the Emperor of Delhi's wrath, boasting that he is the Emperor's judge and arranging his own punishment. Yet that same imperial fear becomes the instrument of his son's downfall: Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition—stamped with Udayaditya's own seal ring—in which the prince appears to be complaining of treason against his father to the Emperor in Delhi in order to seize the kingdom. Instead of delivering it to Delhi, Bhagavat brings it straight to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted it from Udayaditya's fleeing servant. The forged appeal to the very Emperor whose threat Pratapaditya dismissed convinces the king of his son's betrayal and leads to Udayaditya's imprisonment.

While Surma lived, Vibha secretly turned to her to have her hair styled to her own liking, defying the Mahishi's heavy-handed adornment—so much so that the Mahishi, noticing the changed coiffure, blamed Surma for deliberately ruining it and restyled Vibha's hair herself. After Surma's death, that same ritual became the measure of her absence: when the time came to braid her hair, Vibha would sit quietly, waiting as if Surma might still come, but evening fell, night approached, and her hair remained unbraided. Later, when Rammohan came to fetch her, he immediately read her desolation in her appearance—dark circles, no smile, and unkempt hair—concluding that there was no one left in the Jessore palace to care for her. Thus the state of Vibha's hair shifted from a site of Surma's loving, secret attention to a visible sign of grief and neglect once Surma was gone.
